show.name: EXPERIMENTICA 26 – frank r jagoe: Collective Breath (on love and strife)
show.description:
Join artist and Experimentica 2024 alumnus frank r jagoe for a writing workshop exploring embodied engagements with performance.

Writing the live is an act of memory, of temporal shifts, and fabulation. How can writing with/on/around/between performance be a means to practice presence and to become available to the live moment? How is being an audience member an act of participation?

Bringing together pre-Socratic Greek philosophy with contemporary queer ecology and disability studies, we'll consider collective breath, the agency of objects, and the co-contamination of bodies in rooms.

The workshop will be structured as follows: collective reading of short texts; a discussion of the texts and the ideas underpinning the workshop; and two simple writing prompts.

As part of our Writers Circle, workshop participants will be invited to contribute short/raw/unedited responses to Experimentica performances in exchange for a free ticket. Submissions must be shared by 12pm the day after the performance, and will be distributed throughout the building and published on the website.

___

About the artist

frank r jagoe is an artist, writer and sex worker whose work reclaims madness and monstrosity as ways of challenging the exclusionary category of the human. Working across writing, performance and installation, they explore communication beyond rationality and language, foregrounding relationships with more-than-human beings and forms of knowledge that resist Western hierarchies of reason. Their recent book, Significant Others, won the 2024 Prototype Prize and was published by Prototype in 2025. They are currently researching a body of work around rats, sex work, and the control of public space.

About The Writers Circle

The Writers Circle is an open collective of writers based in Wales, gathering semi-regularly to test and exchange new and exper­i­mental writing in response to Chapter’s programme. The group is open to anyone interested in writing on/with/around art. If you'd like to get involved, get in touch with Kit.Edwards@chapter.cymru.

show.name: The Critical Affection Zine Workshop
show.description:
This workshop is part of Incomplete Evidence, a film festival and workshop series presented as part of Chapter’s season of events celebrating the work of Michelle Williams Gamaker.

In collaboration with Dr Meena Saverimuttu (Cardiff University), artist and filmmaker Michelle Williams Gamaker presents a zine workshop inspired by her Critical Affection Trilogy.

Grounded in a deep love for and knowledge of film history, Williams Gamaker’s trilogy resists the colonial and imperialist shape of that history through acts of “fictional activism” and “fictional healing.” In the same spirit of creativity, speculation, and fandom, this zine workshop invites participants to create a zine (a low-cost magazine pronounced as “zeen”) that draws on their experience of Williams Gamaker’s films or other media they enjoy. 

You'll be guided in making an eight-page zine that you can take home.

All materials will be provided, including scissors, markers, pencils, washi tapes, scrapbook materials, and images and other materials related to the Critical Affection Trilogy. You're welcome to bring your own materials as well. 

This workshop is free, but places are strictly limited, so book now to secure your spot.

___

Film history is forged from incomplete evidence, and its incomplete traces suggest a story open to revision. Chapter and Cardiff University present Incomplete Evidence, a film festival and workshop series that concludes a season of events celebrating the work of London-based artist Michelle Williams Gamaker.

Recasting historical actors of colour as “fictional activists,” Williams Gamaker’s films resist colonial storytelling in twentieth-century film. Incomplete Evidence places Williams Gamaker’s work alongside a body of feminist, queer, and anti-racist films that subvert and reimagine film history. In these films, cinema’s incomplete evidence is both positive and negative. It’s a sign of gendered, racial, and other inequalities, but it’s also a site of possibility, opening onto a past that can be reinvented.

Fisherman Stan Rennie has worked the same stretch of coastline in the North-East of England, where the river meets the sea, for over fifty years and the trade has been in his family for centuries. Have the sins of the industrial past come back to haunt the present?Stan finds himself thrown into a battle for the future and he becomes the unlikely figurehead for a grassroots campaign to uncover the truth, managing it in the only way he knows how, with heart, determination and a rich strain of gallows humour. A wry, empathetic documentary by Teesider Jeanie Finlay (Your Fat Friend; The Great Hip Hop Hoax; Seahorse; Sound It Out) about navigating through grief and finding power in community.

Quiet housewife Mona has become a supporting role in her own life; her husband barely acknowledges her presence and their children are on the cusp of fleeing the nest. So when, on an impulse, she auditions for a local production of an original musical, Mona suddenly finds herself in the spotlight when she is cast in a leading role, as Miss Danielle. However, she is unprepared for the theatrical hurricane that is Jerry, her enigmatic director and the ‘biggest name in New Jersey community theatre’. As she continues to be creatively pushed by him, Mona finds herself going to extreme lengths to unlock her character. 

The Debut once again finds the perfect balance between humour and drama that Eisenberg delivered with his previous films A Real Pain (LFF 2024) and When You Finish Saving the World. It’s both sparklingly witty and laugh-out-loud funny, while every scene works to build on the emotional undercurrents and heartbreaking revelations that make the characters so credible. This time, Eisenberg’s talents even stretch to writing the songs for the fictional stage musical. Moore is in her element, giving one of her finest performances, while Paul Giamatti’s Jerry continues his run from The Holdovers as the master of dramedy. Ultimately, The Debut is an elegant and intelligent coming-of-older-age story about how it’s never too late to find our true selves, and the redemptive powers of community and art. Take your seats... show.name: EXPERIMENTICA 26 – Test Dept and Brith Gof: Gododdin Remembered / Cofio Gododdin
show.description:
In 1988, Welsh theatre company Brith Gof and industrial music group Test Dept. transformed a derelict Cardiff factory into a battlefield of water, sand and wreckage. Gododdin became a searing elegy for a nation's identity and its vanishing industrial heart, and still stands among the most important theatre events ever made in Wales.

Now, to mark the relaunch of its soundtrack – remastered and expanded with new material on CD – we're reuniting the artists who created it for a celebration of a landmark in Welsh performance and music history.

BSL interpreted by Claire Anderson.

___

About the artists

Formed in the early 1980s in the UK, Test Dept is regarded as one of the pioneering forces of ‘industrial music’, recognised for their ground-breaking sound and powerful performances. Their fearless and confrontational approach pushes the boundaries of music, art and protest, exploring themes of politics, social issues, and activism.

Brith Gof was one of Wales's most influential experimental theatre companies, founded in 1981 by Mike Pearson and Lis Hughes Jones, later joined by John Hardy and Cliff McLucas. Rooted in Welsh language and identity, it became internationally renowned for ambitious site-specific performances staged in disused factories, ice rinks, railway stations and forests. Landmark productions such as Gododdin (1988–89), Pax (1989–91) and Haearn (1992) fused physical action, scenography, text and music, drawing on Welsh history and on lived experiences of cultural and economic decline. Before disbanding in the early 2000s, Brith Gof helped redefine Welsh theatre, leaving a lasting legacy for contemporary performance.

show.description:
Portuguese with English subtitles

Amanda and Caio are a transgender couple who have shared seven years of love and dreams. When they finally decide to move in together, the intimacy of daily life begins to expose their differences. Caio, romantic and idealistic, longs for emotional stability and a future built together while working at a radio station. Amanda, pragmatic and ambitious, is focused on consolidating her newly launched legal career. 

As routines clash and expectations grow heavier, their relationship starts to fracture. When Amanda meets João at work, unexpected feelings arise, further destabilizing what she and Caio have built. Caught between preserving a shared past and embracing uncertain new paths, Amanda and Caio must confront difficult choices that will redefine who they are — individually and together.

+ Q&A with director Daniel Ribeiro

Daniel Ribeiro is the director of Perfect Endings (2024) and The Way He Looks (2014), which won the Teddy Award and the FIPRESCI Prize at the Berlin Film Festival and was Brazil’s official submission for the 2015 Academy Awards. He also directed the short films You, Me and Him (2008), I Don’t Want to Go Back Alone (2010) (winner of the 2011 Iris Prize), and Love Snaps (2016), which screened at more than 180 festivals worldwide and received 115 awards, including the Crystal Bear at the Berlin Film Festival. Ribeiro is also the creator, writer, and director of the HBO series Todxs Nós (2020). I Am Going to Miss You is his third feature film.

show.name: The Thief of Bagdad + Thieves
show.description:
Classic early Hollywood and British films meet Michelle Williams Gamaker's films, which challenge cinema's colonial storytelling.

Tricked by sinister sorcerer, court advisor Jaffar, the naïve young King Ahmad of Baghdad is deposed and imprisoned. Determined to find a way to reclaim his throne he takes up with a cunning, spritely thief Abu. Fleeing to Basra, the two meet a beautiful princess who is also coveted by Jaffar, and the three embark on a series of fantastical adventures. With sumptuous art direction, and pioneering for its special effects and its gorgeous use of Technicolour, this was highly influential film drawing on international talent and inspiring a generation of filmmakers such who watched it in the cinema with awe. Featuring a sparkling performance from Indian child star Sabu and a pitch-perfect Conrad Veidt, this is one of the most magical and beautiful films of the era. 

+ 

Thieves 
UK | 2023 | 27’ | Michelle Williams Gamaker 

In the second instalment of Critical Affection Trilogy, and Williams Gamaker’s first film in Fictional Revenge, Thieves is a fantasy adventure retelling of the 1924 black-and-white and 1940 Technicolor versions of The Thief of Bagdad. Williams Gamaker reimagines the films’ marginalised characters, Chinese-American actor Anna May Wong and Indian-born American actor Sabu claiming leading roles in her film, uniting as fictional allies, to challenge the racial discrimination of the film industry. Told as a movie within a movie, in Thieves, Anna May Wong is found on set by Sabu, but there is something wrong: she is in black-and-white while everything else is in Technicolor, and both find themselves trapped in their screen-images. Both must navigate the structural violence on set with the help of the Annamaytons and Silver Maiden (in this case, the casting of white actors to replace actors of colour) by joining forces to overthrow the set and those in charge.

show.name: Aberfan: 25 Years of Experience
show.description:
On 21 October 1966, a colliery spoil tip above the village of Aberfan collapsed, engulfing Pantglas Junior School and nearby houses. The disaster claimed the lives of 116 children and 28 adults and was later attributed to the negligence of the National Coal Board. Years later, Aberfan resident Maureen Hughes proposed making a film about the village's largely untold story of healing. Her son, Richard Davies, brought the idea to the Community Video Workshop in Cardiff. Establishing a production base in Aberfan, the filmmakers worked closely with residents, giving the community control over how its experiences were told.

Originally broadcast on Channel 4 and S4C, this moving film is presented on the 60th anniversary of the Aberfan disaster, creating a space for reflection, remembrance and commemoration.

In 17th century France, Father Grandier is accused of bewitching a convent of nuns, including the sexually obsessed Sister Jeanne, with his unorthodox interpretation of scripture. The power-hungry Cardinal Richelieu attempts to eliminate the threat of Grandier by portraying him as a satanist, spearheading a hysteria with the public. Inspired by a true story that laid bare the corruption of the church and collaboration with the state, is presented for the first time restored and uncut for the first time since release. This uncompromising vision from Ken Russell, his defining masterpiece, with incredibly powerful performances from Oliver Reed and Vanessa Redgrave, is an unmissable baroque opus.

show.name: Anushiye Yarnell: Archipelago Movement (Dynamics)
show.description:
Join artist Anushiye Yarnell for Archipelago Movement (Dynamics), an adaptable session inspired by Scaravelli Yoga, Creative Asana, developmental and evolutionary movement patterns, Noguchi Gymnastics, and personal research. This dynamic session will involve moving around the space. 

For ages 14+. 
Please note that under 16s must be accompanied by an adult.

"Exploring forms for feeling
and unfolding your own
personal body sovereignties
through specific and adaptable patterns of movement

Experiential Habitats of:
form and feeling
softness and dynamism
balance and fluctuation
activity and receptivity
resistance and surrender

Inhabiting and translating strength as
relational, reciprocal, experience
(to carry and be carried)
through elemental sensations
density, levity and fluidity.

Inhabiting and translating mobility
fishing for shoals of freedom
and unravelling latent incremental relationships
of fold and flow.”
___


About the artist

Anushiye Yarnell is an interdisciplinary artist whose work spans movement, sound, voice, text, drawing, participation, and alternative pedagogies. Her work congregates in symbiotic, anti-segregative ways of being. She examines the intersections of dream and fantasy realms with ordinary life to find connections between day-to-day experiences of the world and anthropological, philosophical, poetic, and artistic frameworks. She works with tactile presence, reviving sensual intelligence through temporal, ongoing bodies-biographies-mythologies, attempting regeneration despite the rifts and ruptures imposed by colonial civilisations.

show.name: EXPERIMENTICA 26 – Samra Mayanja and Marged Siôn: THE CALL CENTRE
show.description:
A performance programme dedicated to the voice and the unspeakable. Artist Samra Mayanja invites contemporary artists, writers and translators that she's obsessed with to share a new work that is followed by a silly (but deeply serious) Q&A. 

As always, it’s for those of us who freeze in crisis, and a gentle reminder to get unstuck. 

Each event is hosted in another artist’s studio, after gallery opening hours or in a cute little cubby of an art space – it’s iconic (can’t lie). For this special Experimentica edition, Samra invites Cardiff's own Marged Siôn into conversation.

“I’ve been taking singing lessons since 2020 to heal my throat. For whatever reason it kept closing when I went to speak. Perhaps grief or otherwise. Fast forward to 2024, I’m living in London and working in a CALL CENTRE. My job is to listen and to help people locate their pain through language, which in some ways has been the subject of my practise. I feel this job + my wider practise of locating pre-verbal emotion is living in the echo of one of GOD’S JOKES. As in, we are in these bodies with the ability to feel and yet we are illegible to others + ourselves. This is what I mean by the unspeakable, and it feels like a kind of joke, no? This year in particular I’m thinking that, when life gives you lemons, pop them in your studio and wait for the rats to cause your ceiling to smash them which will inevitably create lemonade that you can’t drink (because it’s unsafe) but you can make art about the experience?” – Samra

BSL interpreted by Cathryn McShane.

___ 

About the artists

Samra Mayanja is an artist working across performance and writing. Her practice considers the illegibility of the body and the absurdist impulse to seek what is irretrievably lost. A continuously hopeful but seemingly futile act of searching runs through her work. She also teaches, which she loves most. 

Marged Siôn is an artist and voice practitioner from Cardiff, Wales. Her work engages in voice as a transformative practice by utilising its healing purposes to experience vocal liberation. Her practice explores survivorship, recovery, transformative healing and the importance of embracing imperfection through process. Siôn works and dreams up spaces with those whose voices have been historically silenced to resound collectively for a liberated future. Recent voice work includes Radio Ballads; We Rise; Alter Altar; Atlantic Railton and BBC Proms.

show.description:
A Flickering Space Where the Deed Dissolves is built around the knowledge shared in the issues of TALKER. Using two live-feed cameras and two record players, a collaged story of the process of meeting and interviewing performance-makers unfolds.

Over the course of the performance, details from the interviews are shared as actions, marking these diverse insights into liveness in new ways. The actions accumulate, building a constellation of performance knowledge that explores how a publication might become a live and generative space. 

BSL interpreted by Cathryn McShane.

About the artist
 
Giles Bailey works with performance, using texts, video fragments and choreographies to explore how knowledge and meaning are generated through relationships with others. 

Since 2016, he has published TALKER, an interview zine about performance. Each issue contains a long-form interview with an artist who works in an innovative way with live practice. The publication has featured Ian White, Sue Tompkins, Dora García, Spalding Gray, Kathy Acker, Jo Fong, Paul Maheke, Gustav Metzger, Barby Asante, Miranda July, Agus Nur Amal PMTOH, Bobby Baker, Mayo Thompson, Anne Bean and Martín La Roche.

show.name: Rescoring Film History
show.description:
This workshop is part of Incomplete Evidence, a film festival and workshop series presented as part of Chapter’s season of events celebrating the work of Michelle Williams Gamaker.

This interactive workshop will explore “critical anachronism,” a creative practice of subverting or modulating the politics and meanings of an existing film through music.

Led by Dr Carlo Cenciarelli (Cardiff University) and Barbara De Biasi (Guildhall School of Music and Drama), this workshop will discuss De Biasi’s recent feminist rescoring of Alfred Hitchcock’s Blackmail (1929) along with other examples from early cinema to New Queer Cinema, a body of queer-themed independent films from the 1990s. Participants will also have the chance to undertake hands-on experiments in displacing and replacing film soundtracks.

No specialist music skills are required; anyone interested in film music is welcome!

This workshop is free, but places are strictly limited, so book now to secure your spot.

___

Film history is forged from incomplete evidence, and its incomplete traces suggest a story open to revision. Chapter and Cardiff University present Incomplete Evidence, a film festival and workshop series that concludes a season of events celebrating the work of London-based artist Michelle Williams Gamaker.

Recasting historical actors of colour as “fictional activists,” Williams Gamaker’s films resist colonial storytelling in twentieth-century film. Incomplete Evidence places Williams Gamaker’s work alongside a body of feminist, queer, and anti-racist films that subvert and reimagine film history. In these films, cinema’s incomplete evidence is both positive and negative. It’s a sign of gendered, racial, and other inequalities, but it’s also a site of possibility, opening onto a past that can be reinvented.

She works with tactile presence, reviving sensual intelligence through temporal, ongoing bodies-biographies-mythologies, attempting regeneration despite the rifts and ruptures imposed by colonial civilisations.

bellies! (ap bellies) are back with Power Tools – the first album for nearly a decade from Bristol’s ancient queer diy-ers. With support from Annie Gardiner [TONES]. 

Power Tools weaves musical influences from post-punk, riot grrrl and trad folk that responds to place, loss and the enduring catastrophe of the present. Inspired by visits to Derek Jarman’s house in Dungeness, slipping on the Stiperstones, broken sea walls, stillness found in the Llyn Peninsula, EMDR therapy, Carbon Accounting, Yoko Ono and much more besides. The songs feature bellies (ap bellies)’ characteristic interplay of drums, guitar and dual vocals, deep riffs and poetic lyrics.

About the artists

bellies! (ap bellies) are Nat Brown (The Jelas) and D-M Withers (drunk granny, Social Skills and Punchcutter). We've added (ap bellies) to our name in order to mark a passage of time between then, and between now.  Power Tools was recorded and produced by Annie Gardiner at J & J Studios, Bristol, in 2026 and features artwork by Melanie Clifford.It is available as limited edition full colour cassette and digital download. 

Annie Gardiner [TONES] is a slow core trip through tone bending drones and vocal expression. TONES came into being following several long double bass and vocal improvisations by Annie Gardiner and Jo Kelly for a live show supporting Flower Corsano Duo in July 2025. Two days later, Annie and Jo went into the studio with Jim Barr and performed it once more for the record. The live show is exactly the record, just Annie and Jo reliving an improvisation through lyric-less vocal and bowed double bass. ‘TONES’ by TONES will be released on Crystal Fuzz Records in 2027.

A raw, intimate and visually striking solo performance by Sarah Adedeji, exploring Christianity through the eyes of a Black Deaf woman navigating faith, culture and identity. 

Blending poetry, movement, dance and music, the show interrogates the painful and complex experience of being perceived as “in need of healing” within church spaces. Through personal storytelling and embodied expression, Sarah examines how Deafness is framed within Christian belief, and how Nigerian heritage, British culture and faith intersect, clash and coexist. 

Originally commissioned by Surface Area and previously performed at Alphabetti Theatre, Pray For Me has been further developed under Fuse Theatre’s ‘Lighting the Fuse’ initiative, which champions bold new Deaf-led work. The show then went on to be part of Camden People’s Theatre’s Spring Season earlier this year.

Directed by Harry Jardine with movement direction by Chris Fonseca, and live music and composition from ISRA3L, the piece centres the Deaf experience not as something to be fixed, but as something powerful, political and deeply human.

At once confronting and cathartic, Pray For Me asks urgent questions about access, belief and self-worth - and ultimately reclaims space for Deaf voices within stories of faith.

"IT MUST BE BY HIS DEATH" 

The personal and the political violently collide in Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar, the ultimate story of betrayal, murderous conspiracy and the corruption of good intentions. It is set in Rome in the first century BCE, but it could be anywhere at any time, and every age sees its own reflection in its tragedy. 

Caesar is on the verge of seizing absolute power and making himself king. Opposed to him is a deadly combination of political guile and personal malice in Cassius, and self-deceiving idealism and tortured nobility, represented by Brutus. Add to the mix a volatile mob, ripe for insurgency and violence, and a skilled and charismatic rabble-rouser called Mark Antony, and the result is not ‘Liberty, Freedom and Death to Tyranny’ as promised, but an orgy of vengeful killing, bitter recrimination between friends, the chaos of civil war and multiple suicides.

A powerful and contemporary new production of this tragedy of unintended consequences.

show.name: EXPERIMENTICA 26 – Anne Bean: Iff
show.description:
Beginning with fire, the original light source, Anne Bean collaborates and confounds with changing dark and light, shadows and sparks. Celebrating 25 years of Experimentica, Anne’s performance will create a sense of 25 years appearing and disappearing as they do in people’s memories, as well as how visions are recollected in the spaces and walls of the building and in the histories of experimental performance. About the artist 

Anne Bean is a London-based artist, born in Zambia, working with sculpture, installation, sound, photography, film, video, painting and drawing. Her artistic practice has been pivotal in the development of live and performance art in the UK. Captivated by process and collaboration Bean works as the ‘space-between’ - a receiver, receptor, and conjuror. These strategies enable her to plug into time and timelessness. Since 1970 Anne Bean has presented solo and collaborative projects, worldwide. 

Recently, her work was shown at Tate Britain, Somerset House, the Whitechapel Gallery, Matt’s Gallery, Turner Contemporary, the Hatton Gallery, Paris Photo, Photo London, Cooper Gallery, Venice Biennale, Modern Art Oxford, the Menil Collection, Houston as well as solo shows with England & Co at Frieze Masters and in 2026 at GPS Gallery. Currently, her work is part of Unruly at ARoS Museum, Denmark. She received a Paul Hamlyn Foundation award, 2024.

In this illustrated lecture performance, grasping at absence and images of nothing requires processes of destruction and negation as creative tools. Using looping 16mm projections, narrative text performance, and sound, this performance will connect a constellation of topics around negative themes including, but not limited to: the origins of the phrase “make total destroy;” early 20th century Italian anarchist Renzo Novatore and the “Creative Nothing;” sonic self-erasure and ego death via tape loop; Gaston Bachelard on negation and epistemology; border violence and destituent power; negative psychoanalysis, climate nihilism and the music micro-genre Doomerwave; the artist’s encounter with bureaucratic un-personing examined through the writing of Philip K. Dick; questions about the imperative to make images in the age of AI; and the radical potential of sitting together in darkness.

Mars Saude is a time-based media artist and researcher working in illustrated lecture performances, 16mm film, photography, sound, and critical writing. A Portuguese national raised in California, Saude collaborates with artist collectives in Rotterdam and Bristol, and lives and works in Aberystwyth, Wales.

A spotlight, a drone and a performer move through a theatre occupied by wheels and reflections, where things are not quite what they seem.

The turning wheel becomes a constant force, carrying a history from its earliest forms into the present: a story of invention, labour, movement and violence. The performance is fascinated by the strange relationship between entertainment and power, revealing the curious overlap amongst technologies of spectacle and technologies of war. What you encounter as entertainment or violence can depend upon which side of a border you happen to be standing on.

Part history lesson, part hallucination, Hatchet asks whether the spotlight makes you a star, or if a searchlight makes you a fugitive.

An elaborate ceremony of ritual and absurdity, exploring ancient mysticism, magic and posthuman possibilities.

Relics of consumerism become clustered jewels of finery, as malfunctioning technology, decaying plastics, tangled wiring and shiny fragments are repurposed to form intricately overloaded costumes. Characters clad in these ornate constructions engage in obscure, focused activity within an immersive landscape of illuminated structures and props.

Jennifer Taylor works with live performance, sculpture and film to explore the absurdity of systems, mass production and posthuman futures. She is interested in the remnants of existence: neolithic structures, ancient artefacts, degrading electronics and throw-away novelty ephemera. Overloaded installations and chaotic costumes have a sense of crisis and sublime anxiety that arises from visions of endless landfill and the instability of the technosphere. 

Taylor was born in Wales and studied at the Royal College of Art and the Ruskin School: University of Oxford. She is now based in Cardiff and has completed the Creative-Wales Fellowship at the British School at Rome, the Freelands Artist Programme with g39, and the Wales in Venice 10 Fellowship with Artes Mundi and the Arts Council of Wales.

show.description:
This session is part of Incomplete Evidence, a film festival and workshop series presented as part of Chapter’s season of events celebrating the work of Michelle Williams Gamaker.

Sally Potter’s The Gold Diggers (89 mins, 1983)

The first feature by Sally Potter, director of Orlando and The Party, is many things. The Gold Diggers is, as the director once said, “a musical describing a female quest.” It’s a post-punk exploration of the links between gold, male power, and female glamour produced by an all-female crew. And it’s an inventive and speculative take on film history, with references from Charlie Chaplin’s Gold Rush to the Depression-era Golddiggers of 1933, and a star turn by the actress Julie Christie that recasts Christie’s own cinematic past. Dreamy and non-linear, witty and irreverent, The Gold Diggers takes the glitz and gold of cinema history and makes it into something completely new.

Introduced by film critic and writer Isabella Gullifer-Laurie.

Free tickets to this session include complimentary afternoon tea from 4–5pm.

___

Film history is forged from incomplete evidence, and its incomplete traces suggest a story open to revision. Chapter and Cardiff University present Incomplete Evidence, a film festival and workshop series that concludes a season of events celebrating the work of London-based artist Michelle Williams Gamaker.

Recasting historical actors of colour as “fictional activists,” Williams Gamaker’s films resist colonial storytelling in twentieth-century film. Incomplete Evidence places Williams Gamaker’s work alongside a body of feminist, queer, and anti-racist films that subvert and reimagine film history. In these films, cinema’s incomplete evidence is both positive and negative. It’s a sign of gendered, racial, and other inequalities, but it’s also a site of possibility, opening onto a past that can be reinvented.

Cecilia Barriga’s Meeting of Two Queens (Encuentro entre dos Reinas, 14 mins, 1991) 

Greta Garbo and Marlene Dietrich, two queens of the silver screen, fall in love. Or at least they do in this cult-classic short film by Chilean-Spanish director Cecilia Barriga. A loving act of queer cinephilia. Meeting of Two Queens stitches together moments from some of Garbo’s and Dietrich’s most iconic films – yearning looks, lit cigarettes, exposed legs – into a romantic drama that is the stuff of lesbian dreams. Responding to rumours around the stars’ sexuality, and playing to their cult following within lesbian subcultures, Barriga’s film treats cinema history as open-ended and manipulable. The work of editing becomes a form of intimate contact that can bring together desiring bodies across time and space. And Hollywood emerges as a space in which the spectator’s desires can, and do, reshape its love stories.

Shosho, a young Chinese woman working as a scullery maid in a fashionable London club is given the chance to become the club's main act after the suave club owner Valentine Wilmot sees her sensuous dancing. The Bang Straws
UK | 2021 | 17’ | Michelle Williams Gamaker

The Bang Straws is an aesthetically invigorating reworking of the casting process of Sidney Franklin’s The Good Earth (1937), a film notorious for a white actor’s racist portrayal of a Chinese character. It is the first instalment of her Critical Affection trilogy as Fictional Activism. German-American actress Luise Rainer won the high-profile lead role of O-Lan, the farmer’s wife. To play O-Lan, Rainer wore racist “yellowface”, as so many 20th-century Hollywood and British actors did. Despite Chinese-American actress Anna May Wong’s talent and evident desire to play O-Lan, MGM refused her the lead due to the anti-miscegenation Hays Code, offering her the minor role of sex worker Lotus instead, which she refused. The Bang Straws re-casts O-Lan with a Chinese actor, Dahong Wang, a long-term collaborator of Williams Gamaker’s and reconstructs The Good Earth’s innovative analogue Special Effects, including hyper close ups of locusts and a locust swarm made out of tea leaves.

show.description:
Classic early Hollywood and British films meet Michelle Williams Gamaker's films, which challenge cinema's colonial storytelling.

Set in the globe-trotting fin de siècle class of the playthings of Empire we find Ruby, a beautiful society divorcee with a shady past, who seduces a rich Egyptologist Nigel Armine in London. They marry and move to Cairo, but once living the ex-pat lifestyle she finds herself hopelessly bored, unsuited to settling down with one man. With a queasy inevitability self-absorbed Ruby begins a reckless affair with handsome Egyptian prince Mahoud Baroudi but this latest affair proves to be her undoing. An adaptation of Robert Hitchens’ novel Bella Donna, with exquisite costuming and wonderful performances (including photographer Robert Capa’s only acting role), but especially from Merle Oberon, who gives nuance to her femme fatale, elevating the film beyond its formulaic noir take down of female desire.

+

Strange Evidence 
UK | 2026 | 30’ | Michelle Williams Gamaker 

A genre bending Body Horror/Film Noir, focusing on 1930s British/Hollywood screen star Merle Oberon, who kept her mixed Sri Lankan, Indian and British heritage secret to protect her industry status. She passed as white until her death in 1979. As a contracted star for Alexander Korda’s London Films, Oberon was the so-called resident “exotic” playing stereotypical roles. To transition to leading roles, Oberon falsified her past claiming that she was born in Tasmania to white parents. Behind the scenes she maintained strict control of her image; relying on make-up, lighting, dermabrasion and skin-bleaching procedures. This new work was developed through an innovative process which saw a hybrid installation/film set exhibited at Matt’s Gallery in spring 2025. Alternating between colour and black and white worlds, Williams Gamaker revisits the cosmetic procedures Oberon underwent to maintain this illusion, and speculatively offers the star psychoanalysis to unpack her self-censorship (what the artist calls “Fictional Healing”). The final film weaves these together into a narrative that tries to decode the puzzles that Oberon poses. The capacity for protagonists to speak back is an integral part of the artist’s practice. In the privacy of the Analyst’s consulting room, anxieties, fantasies and the symbolic can be voiced. The project sensitively explores racial stigma, trauma and complex decisions shaped by prejudice and restrictive labour conditions, still impacting performers today. Strange Evidence forms the first part of Williams Gamaker’s new phase in Fictional Healing, following her series in Fictional Activism and Fictional Revenge. It also completes her Critical Affection trilogy with The Bang Straws (2021) and Thieves (2023).

show.description:

A traveller named Lockwood is caught in the snow and stays at the estate of Wuthering Heights, despite the less-than-warm welcome from his host Heathcliff. Awakened in the night by a tapping at the window, what Lockwood discovers alarms the household and brings back memories of a great thwarted love story of passion, hatred and revenge. A gothic masterpiece, beautifully shot by the legendary Gregg Toland and with incredible performances from Merle Oberon, as a yearning and wilful Cathy, with a smouldering and brittle Heathcliff by Laurence Oliver. For many generations this has been considered the definitive screen adaptation of Emily Brontë’s novel. 

+

Oberon
UK | 2023 | 16’ | Michelle Williams Gamaker 

Oberon (2023) was commissioned by BFI, as part of their landmark Powell and Pressburger exhibition, exploring the early genesis of their film The Red Shoes (1948). The work is a response to a photographic series of actor Merle Oberon in the BFI’s collection, taken at around the time that Korda was developing the script for The Red Shoes. Make-up, lighting and cosmetic surgery masked the physical trauma of a car accident in 1937, in addition to Oberon’s complex relationship with her visual identity whereby she passed as white until her death in 1979. These techniques also lightened her skin on camera. Written as a love letter from Korda to Oberon to help her secure The Red Shoes Lead, (the role eventually went to Moira Shearer). Korda speaks the lines of Konstantin – an early version of ballet impresario Boris Lermontov – during a fictional make-up test. Here, spaces of casting/screen tests beyond the archival photographs is a reflective and political tool to question the relationships that extend behind the camera to the individuals (mostly men) who held Oberon’s career and her image in their power.
